content: 1. Chlorobenzene is one of twelve possible chemical species within the group of chlorinated benzenes. At room temperature, it exists as a colorless, volatile liquid with an odor described as not unpleasant, resembling mothballs, benzene, or almonds. 2. This compound has been extensively used in industrial applications for many years, primarily as a solvent and as an intermediate in the production of other chemicals. 3. 4. This assessment was based on a comprehensive literature search conducted in various biomedical and toxicological databases. 5. Chlorobenzene has been the subject of health effects criteria documents prepared by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and similar reviews in Germany. These documents include data from both published and unpublished toxicity studies, often conducted by or on behalf of manufacturers. 6. Chlorobenzene is practically insoluble in water but forms an azeotrope with water that boils at 90°C. It is believed to evaporate rapidly from surface water into the air but may sink to the bottom of still water due to its higher density. 7. The odor threshold for chlorobenzene in air varies between 0.21 ppm and 0.68 ppm, with some sources reporting that its almond-like odor is barely perceptible at 60 ppm. 8. Chlorobenzene is commercially produced by the chlorination of benzene at elevated temperatures in the presence of a catalyst, such as ferric chloride. 9. Historically, chlorobenzene was used as an intermediate in the synthesis of DDT, organochlorine pesticides, phenol, and aniline. During World War I, it was used in large quantities for the production of picric acid, an explosive. Today, its primary use is as an intermediate in the production of nitrochlorobenzenes and diphenyl oxide. 10. Chlorobenzene is also used as a solvent in degreasing processes, metal cleaning, and the dry-cleaning industry. It serves as a solvent for paints, adhesives, waxes, and polishes and has been used as a heat transfer medium and in the manufacture of resins, dyes, perfumes, and pesticides. 11. In the United States, the annual production of chlorobenzene has shown a decreasing trend, but its consumption is estimated to grow at an annual rate of 1-2%. Major manufacturers include Monsanto Co., PPG Industries, and Standard Chlorine Chemical Co. 12. Chlorobenzene is resistant to biodegradation and chemical or physical degradation. It has been shown to bioaccumulate in lipid-rich tissues, such as those of fish and algae. 13.7 mg/m³ in production plants. There are no natural sources of chlorobenzene; most environmental releases result from its use as a solvent. 14. Chlorobenzene degrades slowly in the atmosphere through free radical oxidation. When released into surface water, it evaporates rapidly, but when released to the ground, it binds to soil and migrates slowly to groundwater. 15. In a 1987 accidental release of approximately 450 tons of chlorobenzene into the Baltic Sea, most of the compound sank to the sea bottom due to calm, ice-covered conditions. The environmental consequences of this release remain unknown. 16. Chlorobenzene is metabolized in the liver by the cytochrome P450 system, forming reactive epoxide intermediates. These intermediates are converted to chlorophenols, glutathione conjugates, and dihydrodiol derivatives, which are excreted in urine as mercapturic acids or catechols. 17. Studies have shown that humans may be more susceptible to chlorobenzene-induced hepatotoxicity than mice, as human liver microsomes metabolize chlorobenzene more efficiently through the hepatotoxic 3,4-epoxide pathway. 18. Chlorobenzene is eliminated from the body through expired air, urine, and feces. Urinary excretion of metabolites, such as 4-chlorocatechol and chlorophenols, is the dominant route of elimination. 19. In animal studies, chlorobenzene has been shown to accumulate in adipose tissue, liver, kidneys, and lungs. 20. In humans, chlorobenzene is anticipated to accumulate in fat and possibly in breast milk due to its high lipid solubility. 21. Analytical methods for monitoring chlorobenzene in air include gas chromatography with flame ionization detection (GC-FID) and mass spectrometry. In water samples, the purge-and-trap gas chromatographic procedure is commonly used. 22. 23. National surveys have estimated its concentrations in groundwater and surface water to be less than 1-5 µg/L. 24. The metabolism of chlorobenzene in humans differs from that in experimental animals, with para-chlorophenol being a major urinary metabolite in humans but only a minor one in rabbits.
